module_title: MoA, AoA, and the Core Corporate Doctrines
introduction: This intermediate tier drives into the constitutional documents of a company and the three vital doctrines that govern how a company interacts with the outside world: Ultra Vires, Constructive Notice, and Indoor Management.

core_concepts.title: Memorandum of Association (MoA) vs. Articles of Association (AoA)
core_concepts.description:
- MoA (The Constitution): Defines the company's charter, scope, and relationship with the OUTSIDE world. It contains the Name, Registered Office, Object, Liability, and Capital clauses.
- AoA (The Rulebook): Defines the internal regulations, management rules, and relationship between the company and its MEMBERS. (AoA is always subordinate to the MoA).

core_concepts.title: Doctrine of Ultra Vires
core_concepts.description:
Meaning: 'Beyond the powers'.
- Rule: Any act done by the company that is beyond the scope of its 'Object Clause' in the MoA is absolutely void and legally non-existent. It cannot be ratified (approved) even if 100% of the shareholders agree to it.
- Landmark Case: *Ashbury Railway Carriage and Iron Co. Ltd. v. Riche (1875)*. The company was formed to make railway carriages but entered a contract to finance a railway line. The House of Lords held the contract *ultra vires* and completely void.

core_concepts.title: Doctrine of Constructive Notice
core_concepts.description:
Protects the COMPANY against outsiders.
- Rule: The MoA and AoA are public documents (registered with the RoC). Therefore, the law 'presumes' that any outsider dealing with the company has read and understood these documents. If an outsider enters into a contract that violates the MoA/AoA, they cannot sue the company. The outsider suffers.

core_concepts.title: Doctrine of Indoor Management (Turquand's Rule)
core_concepts.description:
Protects OUTSIDERS against the company (An exception to Constructive Notice).
- Rule: While outsiders are presumed to know the MoA/AoA, they are NOT required to know whether the internal proceedings (indoor management) of the company have been correctly followed.
- Landmark Case: *Royal British Bank v. Turquand (1856)*. The directors issued a bond to Turquand without getting the required internal shareholder resolution. The court ruled Turquand could assume the internal resolution was passed. The company was held liable.

important_entities.name: Exceptions to Indoor Management
important_entities.key_fact: When Turquand's Rule does NOT protect the outsider.
important_entities.significance: An outsider cannot claim the protection of Indoor Management if: (1) They had actual knowledge of the internal irregularity, (2) There was suspicion of irregularity (e.g., an accountant doing a director's job), or (3) The transaction involved a 'Forgery'.

trap_alerts_and_exceptions.explanation: Examiners love this trick: 'The directors entered a contract beyond the MoA, but later all shareholders passed a unanimous resolution to approve it. Is it valid?' **NO**. An act *ultra vires the Directors* can be ratified by shareholders. But an act *ultra vires the MoA (the company itself)* is void ab initio and CANNOT be ratified by anyone.

mnemonics_and_tricks.memory_phrase: Constructive Notice = Shield for Company; Indoor Management = Shield for Outsider
mnemonics_and_tricks.explanation: Remember who each doctrine protects to easily solve practical scenario questions.

exam_strategy_tips: If a CLAT PG or Judiciary exam asks 'Which case established the Doctrine of Indoor Management?', select **Royal British Bank v. Turquand**.
